'''''Calystegia soldanella''''' (syn. ''Convolvulus soldanella'') is a species of [[Convolvulaceae|bindweed]] known by various common names such as '''sea bells''', '''sea bindweed''',<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=250 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=978-0-276-00217-5}}</ref> '''seashore false bindweed''', '''shore bindweed''', '''shore convolvulus''' and '''beach morning glory'''.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Brummitt|first=R.K.|date=2012|title=Calystegia soldanella|url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=16876|url-status=live|access-date=20 May 2021|website=Jepson eFlora|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170829223931/http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=16876 |archive-date=2017-08-29 }}</ref>

==Description==
It is a perennial vine which grows in beach sand and other coastal habitats in [[temperate]] regions across the world.<ref name=nzpcn>{{cite web|title=Calystegia soldanella|url=http://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.asp?ID=2080|publisher=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network|access-date=12 August 2012}}</ref> It is also known as 'The Prince's Flower' after Prince [[Charles Edward Stuart]] who sowed it on the Island of Eriskay, Scotland, when he landed there in 1745 to lead the Jacobite rising.<ref>[E. Dwelly, Gaelic Dictionary (1911)]</ref>

The plant bears trailing,<ref name=Readers/> fleshy stems, kidney-shaped leaves, and creamy-white flower buds and attractive morning glory-like flowers with [[Corolla (flower)|corolla]]s delicate pink to vivid lavender. They are insect-pollinated.

==Distribution==
In North America ''Calystegia soldanella'' is found on the west coast and selected areas of the east coast. In the [[United Kingdom]] it is widespread on the sandy coasts of England and Wales, less common in [[Scotland]] and [[Northern Ireland]]. It is also widespread around the coast of [[Ireland]], the Isle of Man, and Mediterranean coast.<ref>{{cite web|last=|first=|date=2021|title=Calystegia soldanella|url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/calystegia-soldanella|url-status=live|access-date=20 May 2021|website=Online Atlas of British and Irish Flora|publisher=|quote=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210520194113/https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/calystegia-soldanella |archive-date=2021-05-20 }}</ref>

In the southern hemisphere ''Calystegia soldanella'' can be found in coastal areas of Australia, New Zealand, southern South America and South Africa.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:265700-1|title=Calystegia soldanella (L.) Roem. & Schult.|accessdate=5 January 2024}}</ref> In 1973, botanical illustrator [[Nancy Adams]] collected this species on the south coast of [[Wellington]], New Zealand and it was still abundant there 51 years later.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-30 |title=Following a Botany Legend: exploring the life of Nancy Adams |url=https://blog.tepapa.govt.nz/2024/01/31/following-a-botany-legend-exploring-the-life-of-nancy-adams/ |access-date=2024-05-16 |website=Te Papa’s Blog |language=en-NZ}}</ref>
